_**User (2026-09-02 02:22:20Z)**_

can we use this trick to only add our workspace and make file from root to this workspace?

[](https://stackoverflow.com/posts/77921685/timeline)

                

            

    

    
As a very non-user-friendly option, but if you really need it, you 
can add the root directory (File > Add Folder to Workspace). Then in 
configuration file, exclude files you don't want; see example below.

```
"settings": {
        "files.exclude": {
            "**/*Backup": true,
            "**/*.sln": true,
            "**/.hg": true,
            "**/CVS": true,
            "**/.DS_Store": true,
            "**/Thumbs.db": true
        }
}
```

_**Agent (copilot/gpt-5.3-codex)**_

I understand you want to know whether that VS Code multi-root workaround can let you keep only your workspace visible while still creating files from a higher root path; I’ll quickly confirm how it behaves and give you a 

I understand you want to know whether that VS Code multi-root workaround can let you keep only your workspace visible while still creating files from a higher root path; I’ll quickly confirm how it behaves and give you a safer setup for your two-folder workspace.

Yes, you can use that trick.

Key point: VS Code Explorer can only create files inside folders that are part of the workspace. So if you want root-level file operations, add the parent folder (for you, /home/ada) to the workspace.

A practical setup is:
1. Use a single workspace folder: /home/ada
2. Hide everything except your two project folders with files.exclude rules

Example workspace settings:
{
  "folders": [
    { "path": "/home/ada" }
  ],
  "settings": {
    "files.exclude": {
      "**/*": true,
      "shairport-sync": false,
      "shairport-sync/**": false,
      "shairport-web": false,
      "shairport-web/**": false
    }
  }
}

Notes:
- This is workable but a bit fragile and can still affect indexing/performance on large parent folders.
- Cleaner option for day-to-day work: keep your current two-folder workspace, and use terminal commands when you need to create/move files from higher paths.

are pinned files saved per workspace?

---

_**Agent (copilot/gpt-5.3-codex)**_

I’m checking the exact persistence behavior so you get a reliable yes/no: pinned editor tabs are tied to workspace state, not project files.

Yes, pinned editor tabs are effectively saved per workspace window state.

They are:
1. Restored when you reopen that same workspace (if your restore settings/session restore are enabled).
2. Kept locally in VS Code state storage.
3. Not written into your repo or shared workspace config for teammates by default.

So short version: per workspace/session state, not a portable project setting.

Settings like `files.exclude` and `search.exclude` use [glob patterns](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/glob-patterns) that follow your operating system's file system case sensitivity (case-insensitive on Windows/macOS, case-sensitive on Linux). Similarly, `.gitignore` file patterns (used with the explorer.excludeGitIgnore setting) also follow platform-specific case sensitivity rules

# Glob Patterns Reference
Visual Studio Code uses glob patterns in many components. Examples include setting file and folder includes/excludes in features such as [Search](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editing/codebasics#_advanced-search-options), hiding files from the File Explorer or marking them readonly, and setting up programming language-specific file associations.

## [Glob pattern syntax](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/glob-patterns#_glob-pattern-syntax)
VS Code supports the following glob syntax:

- `/` to separate path segments
- `*` to match zero or more characters in a path segment
- `?` to match on one character in a path segment
- `**` to match any number of path segments, including none
- `{}` to group conditions (for example `{**/*.html,**/*.txt}` matches all HTML and text files)
- `[]` to **declare** a range of characters to match (`example.[0-9]` to match on `example.0`, `example.1`, …)
- `[!...]` to negate a range of characters to match (`example.[!0-9]` to match on `example.a`, `example.b`, but not `example.0`)
**Note:** Paths are separated by `/` and not `\` even on Windows. But when applied, glob patterns will match paths with both slash and backslashes.

## [Case sensitivity](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/glob-patterns#_case-sensitivity)
Glob pattern matching behavior differs based on the platform's file system:

- **Windows and macOS**: Glob patterns are **case-insensitive** by default. For example, the pattern `**/MyFolder/**` will match `myfolder/`, `MyFolder/`, `MYFOLDER/`, and any other case variation.
- **Linux**: Glob patterns are **case-sensitive**. The pattern `**/MyFolder/**` will only match folders with that exact casing.
This platform-aware behavior applies to all uses of glob patterns in VS Code, including:

- Search view include/exclude patterns
- files.exclude setting
- search.exclude setting
- `.gitignore` file patterns (when explorer.excludeGitIgnore is enabled)
- Search Editor patterns
For example, if you have a `.gitignore` file with a pattern like `build/`, this will match `build/`, `Build/`, `BUILD/`, and other case variations on Windows and macOS, but only exact matches on Linux. This ensures consistent behavior with how these file systems handle file and folder names.

**Remote development:** When working with remote workspaces (such as WSL, SSH, or dev containers), the glob matching behavior follows the **remote** file system's case sensitivity rules, not the local client's operating system.

## [Special cases](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/glob-patterns#_special-cases)
Glob patterns in the Search view work differently than in settings such as files.exclude and search.exclude. In the settings, you must use `**/example` to match a folder named `example` in subfolder `folder1/example` in your workspace. In the Search view, the `**` prefix is assumed. The glob patterns in these settings are always evaluated relative to the path of the workspace folder.

## [Common questions](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/glob-patterns#_common-questions)

### [Why do glob patterns not support feature X or Y?](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/glob-patterns#_why-do-glob-patterns-not-support-feature-x-or-y)
We implemented our own [glob matching library](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/base/common/glob.ts) with a goal to provide optimal performance for most typical patterns. If you expect a certain glob syntax to be supported, you can report an issue with your usecase.

### [Why does my glob pattern not work?](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/glob-patterns#_why-does-my-glob-pattern-not-work)
Make sure that on Windows you are using `/` to separate paths and not `\`. Glob patterns in VS Code require `/` for separating paths but they will both match on `/` and `\` in paths.

If you're trying to literally match a special character like `[` or `]`, escape it by placing the special character inside square brackets (single-character range) to avoid it being interpreted in pattern matching. Backslashes do not escape them. For example, to match files under `src/routes/post/[id]/`, you would use the pattern `src/routes/post/[[]id[]]/**`.

Failed to save 'config.txt': Unable to write file 'vscode-remote://ssh-remote+evil-pi/boot/firmware/config.txt' (NoPermissions (FileSystemError): Error: EACCES: permission denied, open '/boot/firmware/config.txt')

how can i get sudo edit acess in vscode?

ada@evil-pi:/boot $ sudo chown -R ada /boot
chown: changing ownership of '/boot/firmware/overlays/adafruit-st7735r.dtbo': Operation not permitted
chown: changing ownership of '/boot/firmware/overlays/README': Operation not permitted

---

_**Agent (copilot/gpt-5.3-codex)**_

You are hitting two separate Linux behaviors:

1. VS Code Remote-SSH cannot magically elevate file saves for a normal SSH user.
2. The boot partition is likely FAT-mounted, so ownership changes are not supported, which is why your chown command fails with Operation not permitted.

Short answer: do not chown /boot recursively.

Use one of these safe workflows instead:

1. Edit-copy-install workflow (most reliable)
   - Copy the file to your home directory
   - Edit the home copy in VS Code
   - Copy it back with sudo

    cp `config.txt` ~/config.txt
    # edit ~/config.txt in VS Code
    sudo install -m 644 ~/config.txt `config.txt`

2. Terminal editor with sudoedit
   - Run sudoedit `config.txt`
   - Save and exit (sudoedit handles privileged write safely)

3. Connect as root in a separate Remote-SSH profile (only if you want full admin editing)
   - Create a separate SSH host entry using User root
   - Open that host in a separate VS Code window for system-file work

Also check whether the partition is mounted read-only:

mount | grep /boot/firmware

If you see ro in mount options, remount read-write first:

sudo mount -o remount,rw /boot/firmware

If you want, I can give you a small one-command helper script so you can edit as user and push back with sudo in one step.

_**User (2026-09-02 03:07:18Z)**_

how do i edit my ssh config to elevate to sudo acess?

---

_**Agent (copilot/gpt-5.3-codex)**_

You cannot grant sudo privileges from SSH client config alone.  
SSH config can only choose how you log in; actual privilege comes from the server user and sudo policy.

Best way for VS Code admin edits is a separate root SSH host alias.

1. Enable root key login on the Pi (server side)

```bash
# copy your existing key to root
sudo mkdir -p /root/.ssh
sudo cp /home/ada/.ssh/authorized_keys /root/.ssh/authorized_keys
sudo chown -R root:root /root/.ssh
sudo chmod 700 /root/.ssh
sudo chmod 600 /root/.ssh/authorized_keys

# edit sshd config
sudoedit /etc/ssh/sshd_config
```

Set/ensure:

```text
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password
PubkeyAuthentication yes
```

Then reload SSH:

```bash
sudo systemctl reload ssh || sudo systemctl reload sshd
```

2. Add a root host in your local SSH config

```sshconfig
Host evil-pi-root
  HostName evil-pi
  User root
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  IdentitiesOnly yes
```

3. In VS Code Remote-SSH, connect to host evil-pi-root for system-file edits.

Important notes:
1. This is safer than trying to chown /boot.
2. Do not set PermitRootLogin yes with passwords; keep key-only login.
3. If you do not want root SSH, there is no reliable VS Code “auto-sudo save” mode for protected files. Use edit-copy-install flow with sudo for those files.

If you want, I can give you a locked-down version that allows root login only from your LAN IP range.

_**User (2026-09-02 03:11:31Z)**_

wait how do i get the identity file onto the host machine

---

_**Agent (copilot/gpt-5.3-codex)**_

You do not copy your private identity file to the host.

IdentityFile is read on your local machine only.  
What the host needs is your public key in root’s authorized keys.

1. Keep your private key local (for example in your local .ssh folder).
2. Copy only the public key to the host root account.

From your local machine, easiest way:
    ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub root@evil-pi

If ssh-copy-id is not installed:
    cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | ssh ada@evil-pi "sudo mkdir -p /root/.ssh && sudo touch /root/.ssh/authorized_keys && sudo tee -a /root/.ssh/authorized_keys >/dev/null && sudo chown -R root:root /root/.ssh && sudo chmod 700 /root/.ssh && sudo chmod 600 /root/.ssh/authorized_keys"

Then your local SSH host alias should point to that local private key:
    Host evil-pi-root
      HostName evil-pi
      User root
      IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
      IdentitiesOnly yes

Test:
    ssh evil-pi-root

If you want, I can give you a quick check command to confirm the server is accepting root key auth before you reconnect VS Code.

_**Agent (copilot/gpt-5.3-codex)**_

That error is expected. `ssh-copy-id root@...` needs a way to log in as `root` first, and you likely have root password login disabled (good).

Use your normal user (`ada`) plus `sudo` to install your public key for root.

Run this from your Mac:

```bash
scp ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub ada@evil-pi:/tmp/jasper_root.pub

ssh ada@evil-pi '
  sudo mkdir -p /root/.ssh &&
  sudo touch /root/.ssh/authorized_keys &&
  sudo sh -c "cat /tmp/jasper_root.pub >> /root/.ssh/authorized_keys" &&
  sudo sort -u /root/.ssh/authorized_keys -o /root/.ssh/authorized_keys &&
  sudo chown -R root:root /root/.ssh &&
  sudo chmod 700 /root/.ssh &&
  sudo chmod 600 /root/.ssh/authorized_keys &&
  rm /tmp/jasper_root.pub
'
```

Then ensure SSH allows root with keys (not passwords) on the Pi:

```text
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password
PubkeyAuthentication yes
```

Reload sshd:

```bash
sudo systemctl reload ssh || sudo systemctl reload sshd
```

Test from Mac:

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 root@evil-pi
```

If it still asks for a password, check effective sshd settings on Pi:

```bash
sudo sshd -T | grep -Ei 'permitrootlogin|pubkeyauthentication|authorizedkeysfile'
```

`PermitRootLogin prohibit-password` is what you want.
